idiom_name: Hash registry keyed by AMQP header (Bunny publish/delivery headers)
implementation_notes: The registry is a Hash {token => lambda}, the everyday Ruby idiom, and the metadata channel comes from the AMQP client: Bunny exposes a headers hash on publish and message.headers on delivery, and RabbitMQ's headers exchange can route on those values (with x- prefixed headers excluded from matching unless x-match is set to any-with-x or all-with-x). Ruby's stdlib JSON goes the other way - JSON additions embed a json_class key in the document, which is content-based - so header dispatch plus a Hash lookup is the idiomatic replacement for the classic registry object.
code_sketch:
READERS = {
  'order-created' => ->(body) { OrderCreated.from_json(body) },
  'order-shipped' => ->(body) { OrderShipped.from_json(body) },
}
channel.default_exchange.publish(payload, routing_key: q, headers: { 'type' => 'order-created' })
token  = delivery_info.headers['type']
reader = READERS[token] or raise "unknown message type #{token.inspect}"
event  = reader.call(payload)
pitfalls: A Hash lookup returns nil for an unknown token and Ruby will happily try to call it later; raise at the boundary instead of letting NoMethodError surface deep in the pipeline.
AMQP header values keep their wire types and x- headers are excluded from headers-exchange matching by default, so a token named x-type silently never routes.
JSON additions (create_additions) instantiate classes named inside the payload; enabling them while also using a header token leaves two competing type sources.
